extraction.name: FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech
extraction.description: FLEURS is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. It is designed for tasks including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation, and Retrieval.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna
extraction.publisher: Google Research, Meta AI Research, Carnegie Mellon University
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process starts with the FLoRes-101 dataset, which contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators. The dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences) were split into train, dev, and test sets. For each sentence in 102 languages, three recordings were collected by three different native speakers. Recordings were evaluated by additional workers to ensure they corresponded to the input sentence; invalid recordings were discarded. The process imposed a balance in sex ratio of at least 30/70% when possible.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. The authors plan to fill these gaps in future versions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: FLoRes-101 dataset (sentences from English Wikipedia translated into 101 languages) and new audio recordings of native speakers reading these sentences.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: All recordings are kept as-is, from quiet or noisy environments, without any data augmentations (e.g., SpecAugment, speed perturbation, simulated reverberation). The speech sampling rate is 16kHz. Segments are within 30 seconds.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For text, the original raw transcript is provided alongside a preprocessed version (SRC NORM) and a character-based version (SRC CHAR). Preprocessing steps include NFC and FST normalization, lower-casing, normalization, and removal of punctuation. Words are split into characters. For speech, no augmentation is applied.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Text transcripts were produced by human translators for the FLoRes-101 benchmark. Audio recordings were collected from native speakers. Recordings were validated by additional workers to assess if they corresponded to the input sentence.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers of the respective languages. A balance in sex ratio of at least 30/70% was imposed when possible.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available via TFDS and Huggingface. The authors mention plans to fill missing data gaps in future versions.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender (sex ratio balance was considered during collection).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Performance varies significantly across geographical groups, with better results in Western European and East European languages compared to Sub-Saharan African, South Asian, and CJK languages. This is attributed to the larger amounts of unlabeled pre-training data available for WE and EE languages. Unseen languages in pre-training generally perform worse. Tokenization mismatches affect CJK and some South Asian languages.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Approximately 21.5% of sentences in the first version had no valid recordings. Performance is lower for languages unseen during pre-training. CJK languages suffer from high error rates due to homophones and tokenization issues. Some languages (e.g., Odia) are unrepresented in the text tokenizer used for pre-training models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation, and Retrieval (Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech).
